title: My Coaching Process
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton documents his full instructional coaching cycle, from pre-lesson goal setting to post-session implementation planning, as an alternative to the whole-department CPD day he more usually runs. He argues that department-wide input works only when one high-leverage area is common to everyone; where needs diverge, individual coaching is the better instrument. The cycle begins with the coachee choosing a teaching goal, which Barton insists be narrow enough to act on — 'improve student participation during the Do Now' rather than 'improve student participation' — and held for a whole cycle, a discipline he admits he previously lacked by jumping between focuses week to week. In the lesson he forms a hypothesis about something going differently from how the teacher intends and then hunts a single piece of critical evidence: a count, a verbatim quote, a student's answer to his question, or a photograph of work. The session itself runs praise, then 'the offer', then a model broken into represent, deconstruct, narrate and analyse, then implementation planning that names the lesson, scripts the words and adds a prompt. His worked example follows one teacher, Jenny, through diagnostic questioning across all four stages, and he closes with his sources for video models. The most useful material is his account of his own past mistakes — scattered vague praise and a wandering focus — which is what the structure is designed to prevent.
points: The specificity rule for teaching goals is the load-bearing idea — a goal narrow enough to observe is a goal you can coach toward in small steps.
Holding one goal for an entire cycle is Barton's correction of his own habit of rotating between checking for understanding, behaviour and challenge.
The hypothesis is defined as something diverging from the teacher's intention that the teacher may be unaware of, which is what makes the evidence-gathering purposeful.
Modelling is staged — represent, deconstruct, narrate, analyse — so the coachee sees the whole, then the active ingredients, then why each one matters.
Implementation planning names the specific lesson, scripts the language and builds in a physical prompt, which is what gives the change its best chance of actually happening.
quotes: Most weeks I am lucky enough to be in a school working with their maths department to improve teaching and learning. Often this support involves me watching as many parts of as many lessons as possible in the morning to identify a high-leverage area for development, and then working with all the maths department together in the afternoon with bespoke CPD based on that area.

This approach can be impactful if there is a key area all teachers need to work on - such as boosting the participation ratio or increasing the level of challenge. But when teachers in a department have different needs, an individual coaching approach can be more effective.

This teaching goal remains for a full cycle of coaching so we can take small steps to improve each session. In the past, I have been guilty of jumping around, suggesting we look at checking for understanding this week, then behaviour next, then challenge, and so on.

When I enter the room I spend the first five minutes or so getting a flavour of what is going on. I usually take a photo of the teachers board to frame where we are in the lesson. I make broad notes about what the teacher is saying or doing, and what the teacher is saying or doing.

Then, with the teaching goal in mind, I form a hypothesis about what is actually happening. Specifically, this is a hypothesis about something that is not going to way the teacher intended which the teacher may be unaware of.

Jenny provides a good explanation as to why the correct answer is correct, but I hypothesise that some students do not understand why their choice of answer is incorrect. To test this hypothesis I ask three students who got the question wrong “Can you explain why your answer is not correct?”. No student is able to.

Jenny is going to try this in her next lesson with this class, which is in two days time. We look at the set of diagnostic questions she is going to use and tweak a few to lower the content demands of the maths so students can dedicate more attention to the new routine.
